$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
T(11{v}_{1}+6{v}_{2})=T(-5{v}_{2}).
$$

 

Now, since $T$ is a linear transformation, we have that $T(kv)=kT(v).$ So 

$$
\begin{aligned}T(-5{v}_{2}) & =-5T({v}_{2}) \\  & =-5[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 8 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-35 \\ -40 \\ -45\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, $T(11{v}_{1}+6{v}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}-35 \\ -40 \\ -45\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Let 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 0\end{aligned}].$
Which of the following statements are true?

- $T(kv)=kT(v)$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vector $v$ and real scalar $k$
- $T({v}_{1}+{v}_{2})=T({v}_{1})+T({v}_{2})$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$
- $T$ is a linear transformation
questions.worked_solution:
A linear transformation $T$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}kx+ky \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}k(x+y) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{y}_{1})+({x}_{2}+{y}_{2}) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{y}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is a linear transformation.

As a result, all three statements are true.

questions.problem:
Let 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 4x+3y\end{aligned}].$

- $T(kv)=kT(v)$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vector $v$ and real scalar $k$
- $T({v}_{1}+{v}_{2})=T({v}_{1})+T({v}_{2})$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$
- $T$ is a linear transformation
questions.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}kx+ky \\ 4kx+3ky\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 4x+3y\end{aligned}] \\  & =kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ 4({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+3({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{y}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1}+3{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{2}+3{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Let 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].$
Which of the following statements are true?

- $T(kv)=kT(v)$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vector $v$ and real scalar $k$
- $T({v}_{1}+{v}_{2})=T({v}_{1})+T({v}_{2})$ for any real $2\times 1$ column vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$
- $T$ is **NOT** a linear transformation
questions.worked_solution:
A linear transformation $T$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}(kx)^{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{k}^{2}{x}^{2} \\ k\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={k}^{2}[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is not a linear transformation.

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})^{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}^{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

 

As a result, only statement III is true.

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ 2({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{y}_{1} \\ 2{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\ 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is a linear transformation.

As a result, all three statements are true.

canonical_examples.problem: If $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation and $[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 24\end{aligned}]$ then find $[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, it must satisfy $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ Noting that $[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 24\end{aligned}]$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T([\begin{aligned}12 \\ 24\end{aligned}]) & =T(6[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}])=6T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since we're told that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 24\end{aligned}]
$$

we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}6T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}18 \\ -30\end{aligned}] \\ T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]) & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}18 \\ -30\end{aligned}] \\ T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}.$ If $\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{0}$ and $[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -12 \\ 8\end{aligned}]$ then find $\mathbf{T}(17\mathbf{v}_1+12\mathbf{v}_2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, since $\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{0},$ we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}17{v}_{1}+12{v}_{2} & =5{v}_{1}+12{v}_{1}+12{v}_{2} \\  & =5{v}_{1}+12({v}_{1}+{v}_{2}) \\  & =5{v}_{1}+12(0) \\  & =5{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathbf{T}(17\mathbf{v}_1+12\mathbf{v}_2)=\mathbf{T}(5\mathbf{v}_1).
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{T}$ is a linear transformation, we have that $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v})=k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$ So 

$$
\begin{aligned}T(5{v}_{1}) & =5T({v}_{1}) \\  & =5[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -12 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}45 \\ -60 \\ 40\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, $[\begin{aligned}45 \\ -60 \\ 40\end{aligned}]$

canonical_examples.problem:
Are the following transformations linear?

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's consider $\mathbf{T}_1.$ Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{1}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}(kx)^{2} \\ (kx)(ky)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{k}^{2}{x}^{2} \\ {k}^{2}xy\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}k{x}^{2} \\ kxy\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne k{T}_{1}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\textbf{T}_1$ is not a linear transformation.

Now, let's consider $\mathbf{T}_2.$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{2}[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3kx \\ kx+2ky\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}k(3x) \\ k(x+2y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}3x \\ x+2y\end{aligned}] \\  & =k{T}_{2}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{2}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ ({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+2({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ ({x}_{1}+2{y}_{1})+({x}_{2}+2{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1}+2{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}+2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={T}_{2}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+{T}_{2}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\textbf{T}_2$ is a linear transformation.
